common_name: Superfine Rainbow Coleus (Classic Seed-Grown Multicolor Coleus Strain)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Superfine Rainbow is a long-established seed strain grown for a wide range of leaf colors and patterns within a uniform, compact plant habit.

directions: Plant in partial shade to a few hours of morning sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Superfine Rainbow is a classic seed-grown coleus strain producing a wide spread of leaf colors and patterns, from solid burgundy and chartreuse to elaborate multicolor combinations, on a uniformly compact, well-branched plant that has made it a long-standing favorite for bedding displays and mixed containers where consistent size matters more than a single specific color. Because it is grown from seed rather than propagated as a single named clone, individual plants within a flat will show some natural variation, part of the appeal for gardeners who enjoy a mixed palette. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
North Carolina State Extension — Heirloom Coleus Cultivars

common_name: Plum Brocade Coleus (Trailing Deep Plum-Purple ColorBlaze Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; part of the Proven Winners ColorBlaze coleus series bred for strong trailing habit suited to hanging baskets and container edges.

directions: Plant in partial shade to a few hours of morning sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Plum Brocade bears deep plum-purple leaves with a lighter dusty edge, trailing readily over the sides of a hanging basket or container rather than growing upright, a habit bred deliberately into the ColorBlaze line for spilling foliage displays. Its dark, rich color pairs well with brighter chartreuse or orange coleus cultivars in a mixed container for strong contrast. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage fuller, more branched trailing growth rather than a few long, sparse stems.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant

common_name: Gay's Delight Coleus (Historic Velvety Burgundy Coleus with Green Edge)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; an old heirloom coleus cultivar passed along for generations among collectors of historic coleus varieties.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Gay's Delight bears velvety, deep burgundy-red leaves edged in a contrasting band of bright green, a rich old-fashioned color combination that has been passed along among heirloom coleus collectors for generations, well before the wave of modern sun-tolerant hybrid coleus cultivars took over garden centers. Like most older coleus cultivars it prefers a shadier position than modern sun coleus, since its thinner leaf substance can scorch in strong afternoon exposure. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically through the season to maintain a dense, bushy habit and prevent legginess.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Heirloom Coleus Cultivars
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant

common_name: Religious Radish Coleus (Deep Burgundy-Red Heirloom Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; a whimsically named heirloom coleus cultivar grown for its deep, radish-like burgundy-red color.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Religious Radish bears deep, dusky burgundy-red leaves with a fine darker central marking, a rich, saturated color that has kept the whimsically named cultivar in circulation among heirloom coleus collectors for its solid, dependable dark-foliage display. Like most older coleus cultivars it prefers a shadier position than modern sun-bred hybrids, since its thinner leaf substance can scorch in strong afternoon exposure. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically through the season to maintain a dense, bushy habit and prevent legginess.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Heirloom Coleus Cultivars

common_name: Big Blonde Coleus (Large Chartreuse-Blonde ColorBlaze Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; part of the Proven Winners ColorBlaze coleus series bred for large, vigorous, upright growth.

directions: Plant in partial shade to a few hours of morning sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Big Blonde produces large, bright chartreuse-blonde leaves on a vigorous, upright plant considerably larger than most coleus cultivars, making it useful as a bold foliage anchor at the back of a mixed border or as a stand-alone specimen in a large container. Its pale, glowing color brightens a shaded corner effectively and provides strong contrast against darker burgundy or purple companion coleus cultivars. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically through the season to encourage a fuller, more branched habit rather than a few tall, sparse stems.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
